sweep_summary: Virgin Islands Creole English is not in the catalog and this search of works with stress in the title turned up a single title hit, which is a false positive: Glottolog ref 633563 (Revithiadou, Markopoulos & Messinioti 2014, 'Derived glides and turbid stress', MFM 22) is tagged [vic] only by Glottolog's computerized assignment from the title word 'derived' (stated in the record's language code field, saved as glottolog_ref_633563.bib). The one work that cites it, Baltazani, Kainada, Revithiadou & Topintzi 2016 (Glossa 1(1):23, downloaded from an Internet Archive copy of the Glossa galley since the live site is Anubis-walled; Crossref confirms reference B104 is this paper), says on p. 14 that Revithiadou et al. (2014) examine glide strengthening in Rhodian and Astypalaea Greek varieties; so the paper is about Greek dialect glides/stress. The MFM talk itself could not be located (MFM 22 site gone and not archived; Revithiadou's archived publications page and CV list no conference talks; OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, CORE and scholar.archive. No first-hand statement of Virgin Islands Creole word stress was read in this search of works with stress in the title; our earlier reading in the same directory had likewise found only segmental descriptions and Google Books snippets of Sprauve 1977 mentioning 'primary stress' without a placement rule. Everything downloaded is under with updated (section 'search of works with stress or accent in the title').

new_statements.quote: (a) "... aside prosodic features like stress and pitch which in time can be expected to yield some instructive comparisons, we shall first consider features shared by all three Creole dialects, then one that is found in two of the three, and finally one that is unique to one of the systems." (b) "For the speaker from St. Thomas-St. John this r is unmistakably a sign of Crucian, more so because it is regularly present under primary stress [...], and Crucian stresses a number of commonly used words like mother, brother, and father differently from the other Virgin Island dialect."

new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked under Passage (a): Google Books GData snippet, volume coVOAAAAYAAJ = Microstate Studies 1977, UVA:X000679581) reads verbatim '.. aside prosodic fea- tures like stress and pitch which in time can be expected to yield some instructive comparisons, we shall first consider features shared by all three Creole dialects, then one that is found in two of the three..'; the tail 'and finally one that is unique to one of the systems' is not in q163 but is verbatim in gbooks_feed_q150/q151/same volume). Passage (b): has 'For the speaker from St. Thomas - St. John this r is unmistakably a sign of Cru- cian, more so because it is regularly present under primary stress..' and also q152, q3,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No positional rule is stated anywhere accessible. The primary literature treats VIEC as having English-type lexical (etymological) word stress -- Sprauve speaks of syllables 'under primary stress' vs. weak stress and notes that Crucian (St. Croix) places the stress of some common disyllables (mother, brother, father) differently from St. Thomas-St. John (cf. Smollett 2011 'fáada' vs 'fàadá', i.e. apparently final prominence in Crucian for these words); Faraclas & Ramírez Morales 2006 re-analyse the prominence as an H(L) tonal melody assigned to the syllable stressed in the English citation form. Reading 'lexical (unpredictable)' is therefore an inference (stress lexically specified per word, largely as in the English etymon, with dialect-specific lexical exceptions), not a quoted rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Crucian vs. St. Thomas-St. John differ in the stressing of mother, brother, father (Sprauve 1977); Faraclas & Ramírez Morales 2006 report sentence-final raising of a normally low-toned final syllable (wúmàn -> downstepped H) in Crucian declaratives, i.e. phrase-final pitch effects independent of word stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Sprauve's remark concerns word-level (citation) stress of individual lexemes; Faraclas & Ramírez Morales describe utterance-level intonation over word-level H/L melodies (Crucian only). Sprauve 1977 explicitly postpones treatment of stress and pitch.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.1 virg1240 (iso vic) has no dialect nodes and its coordinates sit near St. Martin; Ethnologue's vic covers USVI (Crucian = St. Croix; St. Thomas-St. John), the British Virgin Islands (Tortola, Anegada, Virgin Gorda, Jost van Dyke) and the Dutch/French SSS islands (Saba, St. Eustatius, St. Martin English). The only stress-relevant statements located (Sprauve 1977; Faraclas & Ramírez Morales 2006; Smollett 2011) concern Crucian (St. Croix) and, contrastively, St. Thomas-St. John; Sprauve notes the two USVI dialects differ lexically in stress placement, so a catalog entry should name the island variety. Saban/Statian English descriptions (Williams & Myrick 2015; Aceto 2006) describe distinct varieties under the same code.

sources.citation: Mahanta, Shakuntala (2012). Locality in exceptions and derived environments in vowel harmony. Natural Language and Linguistic Theory 30. pp. 1109-1146.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: The paper is entirely about Assamese (Indo-Aryan) regressive [ATR] vowel harmony and its morpheme-specific exceptions; 'Assamese' occurs 83 times, 'Virgin', 'Creole', 'Crucian', 'Caribbean' zero times. 'Stress' occurs three times: twice in bibliography entries (Harris 1983; Pater 2000) and once in a general OT remark on positional faithfulness. It is attached to virg1240 only by Glottolog's computerized assignment from the title word 'derived' (the same mechanism recorded for Glottolog ref 633563, Revithiadou et al. 2014, in glottolog_ref_633563.bib).
